claims.text: High-entropy nanoparticle stability is governed by a balance between configurational-entropy stabilization of a uniform solid solution and thermodynamic driving forces for elemental segregation.
At lower operating temperatures, configurational entropy suppresses atomic diffusion.
Lattice distortions suppress atomic diffusion at lower operating temperatures.
Suppressed atomic diffusion maintains a chemically uniform, single-phase state.
Heating toward 1923 K activates sufficient diffusion for selected elements to segregate into nanoscale secondary phases.
The initial material consists of nanoparticles containing at least five metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
The initial nanoparticles are homogeneous solid solutions with uniform elemental distributions.
Grain boundaries mediate atomic mobility and thereby influence the onset and spatial pattern of segregation.
Local lattice distortions mediate atomic mobility and thereby influence the onset and spatial pattern of segregation.
At high temperature, diffusion overcomes entropy stabilization and enables thermodynamically favored elemental segregation.
Cr-V interactions in refractory high-entropy alloys provide an example of a thermodynamic tendency toward segregation.
Diffusion-enabled segregation produces nanoscale precipitates and eventually degrades the uniform solid solution.
Below a material-dependent critical temperature, the nanoparticles will remain a single-phase solid solution.
Below the critical temperature, functional performance will remain uniform.
Above the critical temperature, near the upper operating limit of 1923 K, compositional inhomogeneities or precipitates will form.
Formation of compositional inhomogeneities or precipitates can reduce catalytic activity or alter thermoelectric performance.
The critical temperature and rate of stability loss depend on elemental composition and diffusion kinetics.
Persistence of a uniform single phase without statistically significant segregation or performance degradation near 1923 K would falsify the proposed high-temperature segregation mechanism.
